grading: One point per question; exactly one correct choice; each option includes substantive feedback.

questions.question: Which control must be enabled before NAT-mode multicast policies can pass multicast packets?

options.text: Enable PIM on the ingress interface before applying any multicast policy.
options.feedback: PIM is a multicast-routing mechanism, not the NAT-mode forwarding gate described here.

options.text: Enable IGMP snooping on every VLAN before policy evaluation begins.
options.feedback: IGMP snooping manages receiver membership at Layer 2; it does not enable FortiGate multicast forwarding.

options.text: Enable multicast forwarding in the system settings before evaluating policy matches.
options.feedback: Correct. This matches the documented feature mechanics and its operational boundary.

options.text: Enable multicast routing on the VDOM before creating address objects.
options.feedback: Multicast routing and policy forwarding are separate paths; routing is not the prerequisite here.

questions.question: An administrator uses `dstaddr all` in a multicast policy. Which destination space does that object represent?

options.text: The IPv4 multicast block from 224.0.0.0 through 239.255.255.255.
options.feedback: Correct. This matches the documented feature mechanics and its operational boundary.

options.text: All IPv4 destinations, including unicast and broadcast addresses.
options.feedback: The `all` multicast address object is not a universal IPv4 destination object.

options.text: Only administratively scoped groups from 239.0.0.0 through 239.255.255.255.
options.feedback: The administratively scoped subset is narrower than the documented full multicast block.

options.text: Only the link-local control groups from 224.0.0.0 through 224.0.0.255.
options.feedback: The link-local subset is only a small portion of the multicast address space.

questions.question: A stream reaches the correct egress interface, but receivers see the encoder's private source address. Which policy action changes that source?

options.text: Enable multicast DNAT and replace the destination group with a public address.
options.feedback: DNAT changes the destination group; it does not rewrite the packet's source address.

options.text: Enable multicast forwarding and rely on TTL decrement to rewrite the source.
options.feedback: TTL decrement changes hop lifetime, not source addressing or packet identity.

options.text: Create a static route for the encoder and change its interface address.
options.feedback: A route selects a path; it does not perform multicast source translation.

options.text: Enable multicast SNAT and set the translated source address for the egress path.
options.feedback: Correct. This matches the documented feature mechanics and its operational boundary.

questions.question: After enabling multicast forwarding, a multi-VDOM design begins looping traffic between NPU virtual links. What is the likely policy defect?

options.text: A narrowly scoped policy permits one source group on one downstream interface.
options.feedback: Narrow interface and group scope is the safer design; it does not create the all-to-all loop.

options.text: An all-to-all multicast policy includes both NPU virtual-link interfaces in the same VDOM.
options.feedback: Correct. This matches the documented feature mechanics and its operational boundary.

options.text: The multicast policy uses a UDP destination port instead of all protocols.
options.feedback: A protocol or port match does not by itself create a virtual-link forwarding loop.

options.text: The forwarding gate decrements TTL before sending a packet to the receiver.
options.feedback: TTL handling is not the loop cause identified in the multi-VDOM warning.

questions.question: The FortiGate is configured as a multicast router using PIM. Which design choice avoids enabling the separate flood-forwarding path?

options.text: Enable multicast forwarding and add a deny policy for the router's interfaces.
options.feedback: A deny rule does not change the documented recommendation to keep the forwarding feature disabled.

options.text: Keep multicast forwarding disabled and use the multicast-routing configuration.
options.feedback: Correct. This matches the documented feature mechanics and its operational boundary.

options.text: Enable multicast forwarding only on the ingress VLAN and keep PIM active.
options.feedback: Enabling the forwarding feature remains the wrong path when FortiGate is acting as a multicast router.

options.text: Replace PIM with an any-to-any multicast policy across all VDOM interfaces.
options.feedback: An any-to-any policy increases risk and does not replace multicast routing.

questions.question: A secondary FortiManager is not receiving heartbeat updates. Which transport should the engineer test first?

options.text: Test FGFM management connectivity on TCP port 541 between the FortiGates and manager.
options.feedback: FGFM is the managed-device channel, not the FortiManager HA heartbeat/synchronization port.

options.text: Test FortiGuard update access on TCP port 443 from the primary unit only.
options.feedback: FortiGuard reachability is separate from the peer heartbeat and database synchronization path.

options.text: Test the GUI HTTPS listener on TCP port 10443 between the peer units.
options.feedback: The GUI listener does not carry the documented HA peer heartbeat traffic.

options.text: Test the HA peer connection on TCP port 5199 between the FortiManager units.
options.feedback: Correct. This matches the documented feature mechanics and its operational boundary.

questions.question: Which configuration should be planned separately because it is not synchronized as ordinary FortiManager cluster data?

options.text: Peer-specific network, NTP, local certificates, and remote LDAP settings.
options.feedback: Correct. This matches the documented feature mechanics and its operational boundary.

options.text: Shared ADOM database changes and policy-package revisions from the primary.
options.feedback: ADOM and policy database changes are part of the synchronized configuration state.

options.text: Managed-device database changes committed on the primary FortiManager.
options.feedback: Managed-device database changes are among the data replicated from the primary.

options.text: The synchronized module data and configured deployment-version metadata.
options.feedback: Module data synchronization is a core HA function, not an excluded local setting.

questions.question: A site requires automatic promotion when the primary's monitored interface fails. Which HA mode fits that requirement?

options.text: Use manual mode and wait for an administrator to promote the secondary.
options.feedback: Manual mode requires operator intervention; it does not meet automatic promotion.

options.text: Use database synchronization mode without configuring any failover role.
options.feedback: Synchronization alone does not define automatic role election or a shared address.

options.text: Use VRRP mode with a shared virtual IP and monitored interface.
options.feedback: Correct. This matches the documented feature mechanics and its operational boundary.

options.text: Use a FortiGate HA pair to elect the FortiManager primary automatically.
options.feedback: FortiGate HA elects firewall peers, not FortiManager cluster roles.

questions.question: The heartbeat interval is 10 seconds and the failover threshold is 30 missed heartbeats. What is the nominal detection window?

options.text: Approximately 30 seconds because the threshold is counted in seconds.
options.feedback: The threshold counts missed heartbeat intervals, so thirty intervals at ten seconds equal five minutes.

options.text: Approximately 40 seconds because interval and threshold are added together.
options.feedback: Adding the values ignores that the threshold is a count of intervals.

options.text: Approximately 3,000 seconds because each missed heartbeat is multiplied twice.
options.feedback: The interval is multiplied once by the miss count, not twice.

options.text: Approximately 300 seconds before the threshold is reached.
options.feedback: Correct. This matches the documented feature mechanics and its operational boundary.

questions.question: The HA dashboard shows module data synchronized, but the secondary still has different NTP and network settings. What does that indicate?

options.text: The heartbeat is broken and the secondary is running an old database copy.
options.feedback: This is the expected boundary between replicated module data and excluded local settings.

options.text: The module database is synchronized while peer-local system settings remain independent.
options.feedback: Correct. This matches the documented feature mechanics and its operational boundary.

options.text: The managed FortiGates have not completed their FGFM registration process.
options.feedback: FGFM registration is separate from FortiManager peer-local NTP and network settings.

options.text: The cluster has automatically switched to VRRP mode without a virtual IP.
options.feedback: VRRP mode is not inferred from a difference in local settings.

questions.question: Where is privacy masking enabled for an administrator who should see anonymized log fields?

options.text: Enable it globally in Log View and apply a filter to each saved search.
options.feedback: Log View filters do not establish the profile-level privacy control described by FortiAnalyzer.

options.text: Enable it in each ADOM and assign the ADOM to the administrator account.
options.feedback: ADOM assignment controls administrative scope, not the privacy-masking setting itself.

options.text: Enable it in the administrator profile and assign that profile to the account.
options.feedback: Correct. This matches the documented feature mechanics and its operational boundary.

options.text: Enable it in the report template and use that template for all dashboards.
options.feedback: A report template cannot apply privacy masking across all modules and views.

questions.question: An administrator's profile sets Data Unmasked Time to seven days. What happens to a search spanning thirty days?

options.text: Historical data outside the seven-day window remains masked for that profile.
options.feedback: Correct. This matches the documented feature mechanics and its operational boundary.

options.text: Every record is unmasked because the profile contains a valid data-mask key.
options.feedback: The key permits selective unmasking; it does not override the configured time-window boundary.

options.text: Only the first seven rows are unmasked and the remaining rows are omitted.
options.feedback: The setting is a time range, not a row-count limit or pagination rule.

options.text: The search is rejected because the time window exceeds the profile value.
options.feedback: The documentation describes masking behavior, not rejection of the search.

questions.question: A user can see an original value in the GUI but cannot find it in a downloaded log file. Why?

options.text: FortiAnalyzer excludes masked fields from Log View downloads even for masked-profile users.
options.feedback: Correct. This matches the documented feature mechanics and its operational boundary.

options.text: The download process always converts all source addresses into destination addresses.
options.feedback: Address translation is unrelated to the privacy-masking export behavior.

options.text: The report engine strips every field that has an associated administrator profile.
options.feedback: The rule applies to masked data in Log View downloads, not every field in all reports.

options.text: The log database deletes original values after the user opens the unmask dialog.
options.feedback: The source states that masked values are excluded from output, not deleted from storage.

questions.question: Which view is exempt from the Data Unmasked Time window while custom-view and drill-down data are subject to it?

options.text: The archived log download view is exempt from every masking rule.
options.feedback: Log downloads still exclude masked values; they are not globally exempt.

options.text: The report schedule view is exempt because it uses cached datasets.
options.feedback: Report output is included among modules where selected fields are masked.

options.text: The real-time log view remains outside the time-frame masking rule.
options.feedback: Correct. This matches the documented feature mechanics and its operational boundary.

options.text: The incident timeline view is exempt whenever the administrator has read-only access.
options.feedback: Read-only permission does not remove the time-frame masking boundary.

questions.question: A remote device broadcasts an ARP claim whose sender IP equals the switch management IP. Which detection method is this?

options.text: Active conflict detection sending a gratuitous ARP after the switch boots.
options.feedback: Active detection originates from local switch lifecycle events, not a remote ARP claim.

options.text: Passive conflict detection comparing a remote ARP sender address with switch interface addresses.
options.feedback: Correct. This matches the documented feature mechanics and its operational boundary.

options.text: DHCP snooping rejecting a lease that duplicates a client address.
options.feedback: The described mechanism compares management-interface addresses; it is not DHCP lease enforcement.

options.text: Dynamic ARP inspection validating the switch's upstream gateway MAC.
options.feedback: DAI validates ARP bindings and is not the FortiSwitch conflict-detection method described.

questions.question: When does FortiSwitch actively probe for an IP conflict using gratuitous ARP?

options.text: Only when a DHCP server renews a lease for a connected endpoint.
options.feedback: The documented active probe is tied to local system-interface lifecycle changes.

options.text: Only after an administrator manually clears the ARP table.
options.feedback: Manual ARP clearing is not the trigger for the active GARP probe.

options.text: Whenever a remote switch sends an LLDP neighbor advertisement.
options.feedback: LLDP advertisements do not trigger the documented IP-conflict probe.

options.text: At boot, when an interface comes up, and after a local IP address change.
options.feedback: Correct. This matches the documented feature mechanics and its operational boundary.

questions.question: An active GARP probe receives a reply from another owner of the address. What evidence is explicitly documented?

options.text: A passive-method SNMP trap is guaranteed for every active probe response.
options.feedback: The documentation explicitly identifies a log for active detection; the trap is described for passive detection.

options.text: A system log records the detected conflict on the local system interface.
options.feedback: Correct. This matches the documented feature mechanics and its operational boundary.

options.text: The switch automatically changes its management IP to an unused address.
options.feedback: Automatic address reassignment is not the documented response.

options.text: The switch disables the interface and moves all connected hosts to quarantine.
options.feedback: Port quarantine and interface shutdown are not the described detection action.

questions.question: What should an engineer not infer from FortiSwitch IP conflict detection being enabled?

options.text: That the switch continuously scans every endpoint address in every VLAN.
options.feedback: Correct. This matches the documented feature mechanics and its operational boundary.

options.text: That local system-interface addresses are checked for duplicate ownership.
options.feedback: The feature checks conflicts against system-interface IPs; it is not a subnet-wide endpoint scanner.

options.text: That passive ARP claims can produce a conflict log and SNMP trap.
options.feedback: Passive ARP observation is a documented detection path.

options.text: That active GARP probes run after relevant local interface events.
options.feedback: Active GARP probing is a documented detection path.

questions.question: Which VAP settings are required in the documented WPA3 Beacon Protection example?

options.text: Enable WPA2 mixed mode and disable protected management frames on the VAP.
options.feedback: Beacon Protection is a WPA3 feature and the example enables PMF rather than disabling it.

options.text: Enable only the WTP profile radio and leave the VAP beacon setting disabled.
options.feedback: The VAP property must be enabled; radio assignment alone is insufficient.

options.text: Enable IGMP snooping and DHCP option 82 on the wireless controller interface.
options.feedback: IGMP snooping and DHCP option insertion are unrelated to beacon integrity.

options.text: Enable PMF and set beacon-protection to enable on the WPA3 VAP.
options.feedback: Correct. This matches the documented feature mechanics and its operational boundary.

questions.question: The FortiGate VAP configuration is correct, but the AP does not transmit protected beacons. What should be checked next?

options.text: Confirm the DHCP server has a reservation for the AP management address.
options.feedback: A valid DHCP lease does not prove that the VAP was assigned to the radio.

options.text: Confirm the FortiGate has a multicast policy for the wireless VLAN.
options.feedback: Multicast policy configuration is unrelated to Beacon Protection activation.

options.text: Confirm the VAP is assigned to the active radio in the AP's WTP profile.
options.feedback: Correct. This matches the documented feature mechanics and its operational boundary.

options.text: Confirm the SSID is present in the FortiAnalyzer report schedule.
options.feedback: Report scheduling does not control FortiAP radio/VAP runtime assignment.

questions.question: Which over-the-air evidence proves the beacon contains the documented integrity element?

options.text: An RSN element with a WPA3 cipher suite and no management MIC element.
options.feedback: An RSN element proves security negotiation data, not the Beacon Protection MIC itself.

options.text: A DHCP option 82 value that identifies the access point's switch port.
options.feedback: DHCP option 82 is unrelated to beacon-frame integrity.

options.text: A Management MIC element with tag 76 plus the Beacon Protection capability flag.
options.feedback: Correct. This matches the documented feature mechanics and its operational boundary.

options.text: A RADIUS Access-Accept response that contains the wireless user's group.
options.feedback: RADIUS acceptance proves user authentication, not the beacon's transmitted MIC.

questions.question: Which hardware and software boundary applies to Beacon Protection in the current guide?

options.text: All FortiAP models running any FortiOS version that supports WPA3.
options.feedback: WPA3 support alone does not remove the documented model and firmware requirement.

options.text: Only Wi-Fi 5 access points running FAP 7.4.0 with PMF disabled.
options.feedback: Wi-Fi 5 and disabled PMF do not satisfy the documented support conditions.

options.text: Any FortiAP model if the controller has a current FortiGuard subscription.
options.feedback: FortiGuard subscription does not substitute for supported AP hardware and firmware.

options.text: FortiAP Wi-Fi 6E or Wi-Fi 7 models running FAP 7.6.1 or later.
options.feedback: Correct. This matches the documented feature mechanics and its operational boundary.

questions.question: An authorized host is behind a bridging AP that cannot assign VLANs per client. What does Access Point Management use instead?

options.text: Different DHCP pools and DNS behavior to place hosts into state-based access paths.
options.feedback: Correct. This matches the documented feature mechanics and its operational boundary.

options.text: A unique 802.1Q VLAN on the AP for every connected client MAC address.
options.feedback: The feature exists for APs/hubs where per-host VLAN switching is unavailable.

options.text: A per-host switch ACL installed through 802.1X dynamic authorization.
options.feedback: Per-client VLAN assignment is the mechanism this feature avoids requiring.

options.text: A static route from each endpoint to its assigned registration portal.
options.feedback: Static routes do not classify host state or deliver the documented DNS redirection.

questions.question: A host is absent from the DHCP lease file and uses a static address. Which event can identify this condition?

options.text: The HostRegistered event automatically moves the endpoint into production.
options.feedback: HostRegistered indicates registration state, not a static-IP lease mismatch.

options.text: The StaticIPAddress event can be mapped to an alarm and action.
options.feedback: Correct. This matches the documented feature mechanics and its operational boundary.

options.text: The PortDown event identifies a static address without inspecting host state.
options.feedback: PortDown reports link state, not the absence of a DHCP lease for a host.

options.text: The RogueAP event identifies any endpoint that does not request DHCP.
options.feedback: RogueAP detection is not the documented static-IP host event.

questions.question: A host fails a rescan while still using a production DHCP lease. Why might it remain on production access?

options.text: FortiNAC immediately rewrites the host's static address without a DHCP exchange.
options.feedback: The documented limitation is tied to the existing DHCP lease and reconnect/expiry behavior.

options.text: The AP management feature converts every failed rescan into a VLAN change.
options.feedback: The feature uses DHCP/DNS state control, not automatic static-address rewriting or VLAN changes.

options.text: The host's RADIUS session must expire before any DHCP or DNS decision can change.
options.feedback: RADIUS session expiration is not the stated prerequisite for the DHCP lease transition.

options.text: The existing lease may persist until expiry or disconnect before the isolation DNS path applies.
options.feedback: Correct. This matches the documented feature mechanics and its operational boundary.

questions.question: Which port and device-group treatment is required for the AP-management topology?

options.text: Place the AP uplink in Access Point Management and remove the AP from Bridging Devices.
options.feedback: Correct. This matches the documented feature mechanics and its operational boundary.

options.text: Place the AP uplink in the Registration VLAN group and keep the AP in Bridging Devices.
options.feedback: The registration group is not the documented AP-management port group.

options.text: Place the AP uplink in the FortiLink group and classify the AP as a managed switch.
options.feedback: FortiLink management is a different topology and does not define this AP feature.

options.text: Place the AP uplink in the Isolation group and add the AP as an authorized host.
options.feedback: The AP is infrastructure, not a host that should be placed in the isolation group.

questions.question: What does the unauthorized DHCP/DNS path accomplish for a host behind an AP?

options.text: It assigns a production address and bypasses registration to avoid portal delays.
options.feedback: The unauthorized path is designed to restrict and redirect, not grant production access.

options.text: It forces a Layer 2 VLAN change on the AP without changing the DHCP lease.
options.feedback: Access Point Management uses DHCP/DNS rather than per-host VLAN changes.

options.text: It gives the host restricted addressing and DNS that redirects it to a state-specific portal.
options.feedback: Correct. This matches the documented feature mechanics and its operational boundary.

options.text: It creates a RADIUS machine account and installs a certificate on the endpoint.
options.feedback: Certificate provisioning and machine authentication are separate FortiNAC functions.

questions.question: After directory synchronization, a machine group appears with a `_host` suffix. What does that mapping represent?

options.text: The user group used only after an interactive password login completes.
options.feedback: The suffix identifies the host-group mapping, not an interactive user group.

options.text: The synchronized LDAP compute group used to assign membership to the host identity.
options.feedback: Correct. This matches the documented feature mechanics and its operational boundary.

options.text: The RADIUS client name generated for the switch port during authentication.
options.feedback: RADIUS client identity is separate from directory host-group membership.

options.text: The device-profile group used for FortiGate configuration template assignment.
options.feedback: FortiGate template assignment is unrelated to FortiNAC-F machine RBAC.

questions.question: A customer selects the AD primary group Domain Computers but no machine group is created. What is the correct explanation?

options.text: Primary AD groups are not supported for this mapping; use a normal LDAP security group.
options.feedback: Correct. This matches the documented feature mechanics and its operational boundary.

options.text: FortiNAC-F imports only distribution lists and rejects every security group.
options.feedback: The documented limitation is specifically about primary groups, not all security groups.

options.text: The computer account must be added to the Domain Admins group before synchronization.
options.feedback: Adding endpoints to Domain Admins is not a supported or safe requirement.

options.text: The RADIUS server must be changed from MSCHAPv2 to PAP before group creation.
options.feedback: Changing RADIUS authentication protocol does not make a primary AD group importable.

questions.question: Which EAP-TLS evidence is most useful when machine authentication fails after certificate replacement?

options.text: The DHCP lease duration, gateway ARP cache, and endpoint DNS search suffix.
options.feedback: DHCP and ARP evidence do not validate the EAP-TLS client certificate chain.

options.text: The presented client certificate, trusted root chain, and hostname attribute mapping.
options.feedback: Correct. This matches the documented feature mechanics and its operational boundary.

options.text: The FortiGate policy hit count, NAT session table, and IPsec tunnel status.
options.feedback: Firewall and VPN state are not the certificate validation path at the NAC RADIUS server.

options.text: The FortiAnalyzer report schedule, archive retention, and administrator profile.
options.feedback: FortiAnalyzer reporting settings do not validate machine EAP-TLS credentials.

questions.question: When is the Client Certificate Attribute enhancement available for machine authentication?

options.text: It is available in every FortiNAC-F release before 7.6.0 by default.
options.feedback: The release note identifies the enhancement as 7.6.3 and later.

options.text: It is available only when the endpoint uses a static IPv4 address.
options.feedback: Static addressing is unrelated to certificate subject attribute extraction.

options.text: It is available only for PEAP-MSCHAPv2 and never for EAP-TLS.
options.feedback: The setting is associated with EAP-TLS certificate identity, not PEAP-only authentication.

options.text: Starting in FortiNAC-F 7.6.3, when the certificate subject needs hostname extraction.
options.feedback: Correct. This matches the documented feature mechanics and its operational boundary.

questions.question: Which release introduced FIDO authentication for IdP-initiated SAML login?

options.text: FortiAuthenticator 7.4.0 introduced FIDO for every SP-initiated SAML flow.
options.feedback: The feature is documented in the 8.0.2 release notes, not 7.4.0.

options.text: FortiAuthenticator 8.0.0 replaced SAML assertions with direct RADIUS tokens.
options.feedback: SAML assertions remain part of the IdP-to-SP transaction.

options.text: FortiAuthenticator 8.0.2 introduced the IdP-initiated FIDO authentication option.
options.feedback: Correct. This matches the documented feature mechanics and its operational boundary.

options.text: FortiAuthenticator 8.0.3 removed FIDO and requires password-only IdP login.
options.feedback: The current 8.0.3 SAML IdP guide retains the FIDO flow.

questions.question: A FIDO-required IdP login begins with a username-only page. What is the purpose of that first step?

options.text: It creates the SAML assertion before the user completes authentication.
options.feedback: The assertion is generated after successful IdP authentication and SP selection.

options.text: It bypasses the FIDO authenticator and forwards credentials directly to the SP.
options.feedback: The page is the beginning of the configured factor flow, not a bypass.

options.text: It identifies the user so FortiAuthenticator can apply the configured FIDO/password method.
options.feedback: Correct. This matches the documented feature mechanics and its operational boundary.

options.text: It discovers the SP's ACS URL by querying the user's DNS resolver.
options.feedback: ACS metadata is part of SP configuration, not discovered through user DNS.

questions.question: A user authenticates successfully with FIDO but does not see a required SP in the portal. What should be checked?

options.text: The FortiGate multicast policy and the user's source NAT address.
options.feedback: FIDO proves the IdP factor; SP visibility still depends on SP configuration and authorization.

options.text: The SP's IdP-initiated assertion-response setting and user authorization filters.
options.feedback: Correct. This matches the documented feature mechanics and its operational boundary.

options.text: The FortiPAM RDP security level and target KDC address.
options.feedback: Multicast policy and NAT do not control SAML service-provider visibility.

options.text: The FortiSwitch IP conflict trap and the AP Beacon Protection flag.
options.feedback: RDP Kerberos settings do not control FortiAuthenticator SP selection.

questions.question: What does a successful FIDO challenge establish in an IdP-initiated SAML flow?

options.text: The user passed the configured IdP authentication step, not that the SP accepted the assertion.
options.feedback: Correct. This matches the documented feature mechanics and its operational boundary.

options.text: The service provider has already authorized every resource in its application.
options.feedback: Resource authorization is an SP decision that occurs after assertion delivery.

options.text: The browser has verified the SP's audience and ACS URL before the assertion exists.
options.feedback: The SP validates its assertion conditions after the IdP sends the response.

options.text: The FortiAuthenticator has bypassed signature validation at the service provider.
options.feedback: FIDO does not remove the SP's signature and assertion validation requirements.

questions.question: Which RDP security level must be selected before FortiPAM's Kerberos option takes effect?

options.text: Select TLS so the browser-based Web RDP launcher uses certificate authentication.
options.feedback: The Kerberos option is explicitly tied to NLA, not the Web RDP TLS mode.

options.text: Select Best Effort so the target can choose NTLM or Kerberos without configuration.
options.feedback: Best Effort does not explicitly force the Kerberos NLA path.

options.text: Select RDP so the connection skips NLA and requests a Kerberos ticket later.
options.feedback: The RDP security level bypasses NLA, so the Kerberos NLA option cannot apply.

options.text: Select Network Level Authentication so the native launcher uses CredSSP.
options.feedback: Correct. This matches the documented feature mechanics and its operational boundary.

questions.question: The KDC Address field is empty. How does FortiPAM locate the Key Distribution Center?

options.text: It queries the target's default gateway for an active Kerberos server.
options.feedback: The gateway is not a Kerberos service-discovery mechanism.

options.text: It discovers the KDC through DNS SRV records for the Kerberos realm.
options.feedback: Correct. This matches the documented feature mechanics and its operational boundary.

options.text: It uses the first DNS A record returned for the RDP target hostname.
options.feedback: A target A record resolves the host, not necessarily the realm's KDC.

options.text: It broadcasts a UDP probe on port 88 across the target subnet.
options.feedback: Kerberos KDC discovery uses DNS SRV, not a subnet-wide broadcast scan.

questions.question: A team wants Kerberos for browser-based Web RDP sessions. What is the documented limitation?

options.text: Kerberos support applies only to Web RDP when TCP forwarding is enabled.
options.feedback: The documentation explicitly limits Kerberos to native RDP, not Web RDP.

options.text: Kerberos support applies to every launcher if the secret uses an AD template.
options.feedback: An AD template does not remove the native-launcher limitation.

options.text: Kerberos support applies only to the native RDP launcher.
options.feedback: Correct. This matches the documented feature mechanics and its operational boundary.

options.text: Kerberos support applies only to VNC and SSH sessions through the proxy.
options.feedback: VNC and SSH do not use the RDP NLA Kerberos flow.

questions.question: What changes when TCP Forwarding is enabled for a native RDP secret?

options.text: The session forces Kerberos and disables the need for a target domain.
options.feedback: TCP forwarding does not force Kerberos or remove the realm dependency.

options.text: The session changes the target's KDC port from 88 to 443 automatically.
options.feedback: The KDC port is not changed by TCP forwarding.

options.text: The session switches from NLA to Web RDP while retaining clipboard controls.
options.feedback: The documented TCP-forwarding path removes several RDP controls rather than retaining them.

options.text: The session follows the generic TCP-forwarding path and RDP security controls are unavailable.
options.feedback: Correct. This matches the documented feature mechanics and its operational boundary.

questions.question: An administrator cannot find Federated Search in a non-ClickHouse deployment. What is the likely reason?

options.text: Federated Search is supported for ClickHouse deployments, not the non-ClickHouse topology.
options.feedback: Correct. This matches the documented feature mechanics and its operational boundary.

options.text: Federated Search requires a PostgreSQL-only deployment with no ClickHouse nodes.
options.feedback: The feature is documented as ClickHouse-only, not PostgreSQL-only.

options.text: Federated Search is enabled only when every Collector runs Windows agents.
options.feedback: Collector operating systems do not define the Federated Search deployment requirement.

options.text: Federated Search is hidden until the FortiSIEM Supervisor has two HA peers.
options.feedback: HA peer count is not the documented enablement condition.

questions.question: A Federated Search dataset exists but the query returns no rows for a known source IP. Which configuration is the first mapping check?

options.text: Confirm the FortiSIEM incident ID maps to the external table's timestamp column.
options.feedback: Incident ID and timestamp are different observable types and do not validate Source IP mapping.

options.text: Confirm the external table's password maps to the ClickHouse result schema.
options.feedback: Credentials are configured on the provider, not mapped as a result-column observable.

options.text: Confirm the Collector hostname maps to the browser's source MAC address.
options.feedback: Collector hostname and browser MAC are unrelated to the Source IP observable mapping.

options.text: Confirm the FortiSIEM Source IP observable maps to the external table's IP column.
options.feedback: Correct. This matches the documented feature mechanics and its operational boundary.

questions.question: What is the correct setup order for a new external data source?

options.text: Create the search, export a case, then add provider credentials and table mappings.
options.feedback: A search cannot query a provider dataset that has not been configured.

options.text: Map observables first, deploy an empty provider, then create the external datastore.
options.feedback: Mappings require a defined external dataset and its columns.

options.text: Configure provider credentials, define datastore/table, map observables, then execute a search.
options.feedback: Correct. This matches the documented feature mechanics and its operational boundary.

options.text: Create a ClickHouse table manually, disable the provider, then add the data source.
options.feedback: Manual ClickHouse tables and disabled providers are not the documented setup workflow.

questions.question: Why can a Federated Search result later be queried from Advanced Search?

options.text: The result is written back into the external source table as a permanent record.
options.feedback: Federated Search reads external sources; it does not write results back into them.

options.text: The executed federated result is stored in ClickHouse for reuse by Advanced Search.
options.feedback: Correct. This matches the documented feature mechanics and its operational boundary.

options.text: The browser caches the JSON response and Advanced Search reads the browser cache.
options.feedback: Browser cache is not the FortiSIEM result persistence mechanism.

options.text: The result is converted into a FortiGate traffic log and forwarded to the Supervisor.
options.feedback: FortiGate traffic logging is unrelated to Federated Search result storage.

questions.question: The provider connection test succeeds, but searches return wrong values for Destination IP. What is the most likely defect?

options.text: The Destination IP observable is mapped to the wrong external column or data type.
options.feedback: Correct. This matches the documented feature mechanics and its operational boundary.

options.text: The provider password is invalid even though its connection test succeeds.
options.feedback: A successful provider test makes invalid credentials less likely than a mapping defect.

options.text: The ClickHouse cluster has no Supervisor heartbeat on TCP port 5199.
options.feedback: TCP 5199 is FortiManager HA heartbeat, not FortiSIEM federated search.

options.text: The incident's source IP was translated by a FortiGate multicast policy.
options.feedback: Multicast NAT does not change how an external column is mapped to an observable.

questions.question: A provider definition was edited, but one ClickHouse data node still cannot query it. What deployment step should be verified?

options.text: Apply or deploy the provider and dataset configuration to the ClickHouse data nodes.
options.feedback: Correct. This matches the documented feature mechanics and its operational boundary.

options.text: Restart every Collector and wait for its Windows machine account to synchronize.
options.feedback: Provider deployment is the step that distributes the configuration to data nodes.

options.text: Recreate the incident and change the source IP observable to a user field.
options.feedback: Changing an incident field does not deploy provider credentials or dataset mappings.

options.text: Disable Advanced Search so the new provider becomes the default query engine.
options.feedback: Advanced Search is a consumer of results, not the provider configuration deployment control.

questions.question: Which traffic is covered by the HTTP/3 QUIC inspection action described in the FortiSASE guide?

options.text: All proxy users and agentless browser sessions, but not managed FortiClient endpoints.
options.feedback: The guide explicitly excludes proxy-policy traffic and includes agent/edge traffic.

options.text: Only traffic from FortiGate SPA hubs, excluding all remote agents and Edge devices.
options.feedback: The feature applies to agent and edge devices, not only SPA hub traffic.

options.text: Only DNS and RADIUS control traffic, excluding user web browsing sessions.
options.feedback: DNS and RADIUS are separate control-plane services, not the HTTP/3 web-traffic scope.

options.text: Agent and authorized Edge-device traffic, not proxy-policy traffic.
options.feedback: Correct. This matches the documented feature mechanics and its operational boundary.

questions.question: A browser uses QUIC but the administrator wants inspection through the HTTP/2 path. Which action is appropriate?

options.text: Bypass HTTP/3 so the browser is forced to reconnect through HTTP/2 inspection.
options.feedback: Bypass allows HTTP/3 without inspection; it does not force an HTTP/2 fallback.

options.text: Block HTTP/3 QUIC so most clients fall back to HTTP/2 over TLS.
options.feedback: Correct. This matches the documented feature mechanics and its operational boundary.

options.text: Inspect HTTP/3 but disable the browser's TCP stack to force TLS over UDP.
options.feedback: Disabling TCP would break the fallback transport rather than force it.

options.text: Allow QUIC and remove the SSL inspection profile from the security profile group.
options.feedback: Removing SSL inspection removes the inspection path instead of enforcing a controlled fallback.

questions.question: The administrator sees UDP/443 sessions but cannot prove the browser negotiated HTTP/3. What is the strongest client-side check?

options.text: Check only the endpoint's default gateway and assume every UDP/443 session is QUIC.
options.feedback: UDP/443 can carry other traffic; the negotiated HTTP protocol must be verified.

options.text: Check the FortiSASE DNS rule and infer HTTP/3 from a successful hostname lookup.
options.feedback: DNS resolution does not identify the HTTP application protocol.

options.text: Inspect the browser's network protocol column for `h3` rather than assuming UDP/443 is sufficient.
options.feedback: Correct. This matches the documented feature mechanics and its operational boundary.

options.text: Check the proxy user's email domain and infer HTTP/3 from its authentication result.
options.feedback: User identity does not prove the browser's negotiated transport protocol.

questions.question: The first Performance SLA server becomes unreachable, but the second remains healthy. What should the link monitor do?

options.text: Mark the member failed immediately and withdraw its routes after one missed probe.
options.feedback: The dual-server design prevents one target outage from declaring the link down.

options.text: Switch the probe target to the second server and keep the member usable.
options.feedback: Correct. This matches the documented feature mechanics and its operational boundary.

options.text: Continue probing only the first server until the recovery timer expires.
options.feedback: The monitor uses the secondary target when the first is unavailable.

options.text: Create a second independent SLA automatically and load balance between both servers.
options.feedback: A second configured server is a fallback target, not an automatically created SLA.

questions.question: When does a single dual-server Performance SLA declare its health check failed?

options.text: When both configured probe servers are unavailable for that health check.
options.feedback: Correct. This matches the documented feature mechanics and its operational boundary.

options.text: When the first server is unavailable, even if the secondary server responds.
options.feedback: The secondary target exists to avoid false link-down from a single server failure.

options.text: When latency exceeds the target on either server for one measurement interval.
options.feedback: SLA target thresholds are separate from server reachability and failure confirmation.

options.text: When the second server has a different IP address from the first server.
options.feedback: Different server addresses are expected for redundant probe targets.

questions.question: The GUI shows a green server-response arrow, but the SLA target is not met. What does the arrow prove?

options.text: The member meets every SLA threshold and all associated routes are installed.
options.feedback: A response indicator is not a substitute for the measured quality values and SLA thresholds.

options.text: The first server is active and the second server is unreachable.
options.feedback: The arrow does not identify that the secondary target is unreachable.

options.text: The route has been withdrawn and the member is no longer in load balancing.
options.feedback: A responding server does not mean the member route has been withdrawn.
